summary: NASA Earth Intelligence Jukebox is an interactive web app that lets people see, hear and explore NASA Earth data. Its core feature, the Earth Jukebox, analyses NASA satellite imagery (NASA GIBS layers such as night lights, sea surface temperature, aerosols and vegetation) in the browser and turns colour, brightness, saturation and bright-pixel density into live generated music. Users can choose any country or city, pick a mood, or upload their own Earth visualization frame. Each frame also gets an automatic text description, and the controls work with a keyboard and screen reader, so blind and low-vision users can experience Earth science that is usually only visual. Around the Jukebox, the app adds NASA POWER climate charts, a Time Machine for comparing years, alerts, a what-if simulator and learning missions. It matters because it makes NASA Earth data accessible, engaging and easier to understand for everyone. Built with React, Flask and SQLite by Team TechHackers.
details:
What it does and how it works
NASA Earth Intelligence Jukebox is a web app that lets people see, hear and explore NASA Earth data. In the Earth Jukebox, the user picks a NASA GIBS imagery layer (night lights, sea surface temperature, aerosols, vegetation, fires or true colour), a place and a mood. The browser analyses the image in 32 vertical strips and generates music live with the Web Audio API. Colour sets the chord on a musical scale, brightness sets loudness and pitch, saturation shapes the tone, bright-pixel density sets rhythm, and the height of bright features sets the melody. A place’s mean temperature from NASA POWER also shifts the musical key, so different places sound different. Users can also upload their own Earth visualization frame. Each frame gets an automatic text description.

Around the Jukebox, users can search any country, state or city and see NASA POWER temperature, rainfall and humidity charts. They can compare satellite imagery between two years in a Time Machine, see temperature, rainfall and fire alerts, run a what-if simulator, view a transparent custom Earth Health Score, and complete data missions.

Benefits and impact
Most Earth science visualizations are visual only, which excludes blind and low-vision people and makes the data hard for everyone to interpret. Turning imagery into sound, with text descriptions and keyboard-friendly controls, gives more people a way into NASA Earth data. It also makes the data more engaging for students and the public.

Tools and technology
React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet and Recharts on the frontend. Python Flask, Pandas, NumPy and SQLite on the backend. The Web Audio API for sound. NASA POWER, NASA GIBS and NASA FIRMS for data, and OpenStreetMap for place search.

Creativity
The project joins sight, sound and data in one tool. The sound is generated live from the pixels, with musical scales keeping it pleasant, so any NASA frame can become music.

What we considered
Accessibility, honesty about limits and ease of use. The health score and simulator are clearly labelled as our own illustrative tools, not NASA measurements or predictions. The “Ask Earth AI” assistant is rule-based and answers only from retrieved NASA data, naming its source. The sound mapping is an artistic design, not a calibrated measurement. Fire data needs a free NASA FIRMS key.
